questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Coordination number read from a formula
questions.learningObjective: read a coordination number from a complex formula
questions.stem: A complex has the formula [Co(NH3)6]3+. How is its coordination number defined and what is its value here?

options.text: the number of ligands, which is 6, since each ammine counts once
options.misconception: counts ligands rather than the donor atoms each one presents

options.text: the number of metal electrons, which is 6 from the group number
options.misconception: counts valence electrons of the metal as though they were coordination sites

options.text: the number of donor atoms attached, which is 6 here
the number of bonds including the internal ones of each ligand
options.misconception: counts the hydrogen bonds inside the ammine ligands as coordination

questions.explanation: The coordination number is the number of donor atoms tied to the central metal by coordinate bonds, and an ammine ligand donates exactly one, the nitrogen of its lone pair. Six ammines therefore give a coordination number of 6, and in this case ligands and donor atoms happen to give the same number. They need not: a bidentate ligand such as ethylenediamine donates two atoms from one molecule, so a complex with three of them still has a coordination number of 6, and that is exactly what makes it a chelate. Counting internal bonds of the ligands, or the metal's valence electrons, gives numbers with no geometric meaning at all.
questions.hint: Count the atoms that actually donate a lone pair to the metal, not the ligand molecules.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Denticity of a polydentate ligand
questions.learningObjective: state the denticity of a polydentate ligand and its consequence
questions.stem: The ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion binds one metal through two nitrogen atoms and four carboxylate oxygens. How is that described?

options.text: hexadentate, since it donates six separate donor atoms
bidentate, since it holds one metal through two nitrogen atoms
options.misconception: counts only the nitrogen donors and ignores the four oxygens

options.text: monodentate, since it donates only the negatively charged oxygens
options.misconception: ignores the neutral amine nitrogens and counts only anionic donors

options.text: tetradentate, since only the four carboxylate groups coordinate
options.misconception: counts the carboxylate groups and forgets that the amines also coordinate

questions.explanation: Denticity counts the separate donor atoms a single ligand offers, and this ligand offers two amine nitrogens and four carboxylate oxygens, so it is hexadentate and forms one five-membered ring on each side of the metal. That is the whole reason it is used in analysis: one molecule of ligand ties up one metal ion completely, so the reaction is 1 to 1 and needs no indicator to detect the end point. A ligand that binds through a single atom is monodentate, and one that bridges through two is bidentate, so both of the wrong counts in the options are counting a subset of the donors.
questions.hint: Count every atom that donates a lone pair, whichever part of the ligand it sits on.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Oxidation state from the complex formula
questions.learningObjective: find the metal oxidation state from a complex formula
questions.stem: In the complex [Fe(CN)6]4-, every cyanido ligand carries a charge of 1-. What is the oxidation state of the iron?

options.text: plus 6, because six ligands each contribute one positive charge
options.misconception: adds the ligand charges to the metal instead of subtracting them

options.text: minus 2, because the overall charge is negative
options.misconception: takes the sign of the complex charge as the oxidation state of the metal

options.text: plus 4, because the charge on the complex is 4-
options.misconception: reads the magnitude of the complex charge as the metal oxidation state

options.text: plus 2, because six minus ones leave a metal of plus two

questions.explanation: Write the sum of oxidation states equal to the charge on the complex: x + 6 x (-1) = -4, so x = +2. The ligands are counted with a negative sign because cyanido carries a charge of 1-, and the whole point of the exercise is that the metal must make up the difference. Neutral ligands such as ammonia or water contribute nothing, so a complex such as [Co(NH3)6]3+ puts the entire 3+ on the metal. The oxidation state is not the same as the formal charge on the metal in a Lewis structure, and it is not the total charge of the complex, which is the sum of all the parts.
questions.hint: Sum of the ligand charges plus the metal oxidation state equals the complex charge.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Monodentate against bidentate ligands
questions.learningObjective: distinguish monodentate and bidentate ligands by their donors
questions.stem: Ammonia and ethylenediamine both coordinate through nitrogen. What distinguishes them?

options.text: ammonia is monodentate and ethylenediamine is bidentate
ammonia is bidentate and ethylenediamine is monodentate
options.misconception: swaps the denticity of the two ligands

options.text: both are monodentate, since each nitrogen donates one lone pair
options.misconception: ignores that ethylenediamine carries a second, distant nitrogen

options.text: both are bidentate, since each molecule carries two nitrogen atoms
options.misconception: counts nitrogen atoms present in the formula rather than those able to donate

questions.explanation: Denticity counts the donor atoms a ligand can reach the metal with, not the donor atoms it contains. Ammonia has one nitrogen with a lone pair, so it is monodentate. Ethylenediamine, H2N-CH2-CH2-NH2, has a second nitrogen on the far end of a two-carbon chain, and the chain is long enough that both can sit on the same metal, so it is bidentate and closes a five-membered ring. The two nitrogens being the same element is irrelevant; what matters is whether a single molecule can present both to one metal, which is also why a much longer diamine, with too long a chain, stops chelating.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate donor atoms one molecule can offer to the same metal centre.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Charge carried by a neutral ligand
questions.learningObjective: decide how a neutral ligand affects the complex charge
questions.stem: A salt is written [Cu(NH3)4]SO4. Which statement about the charges is correct?

options.text: ammonia is neutral, so copper is 2+ and sulfate is the counter-ion
ammonia carries 1-, so copper is 6+ and the sulfate is a ligand
options.misconception: gives neutral ammonia a charge it does not have

options.text: sulfate is a ligand, so the coordination number is 5 rather than 4
options.misconception: counts the counter-ion as a ligand and so inflates the coordination number

options.text: the complex is neutral, so the sulfate must be part of the coordination sphere
options.misconception: ignores the sulfate outside the brackets, which is not neutral

questions.explanation: Everything inside the square brackets is the coordination sphere, and everything outside is a counter-ion that balances the charge. Ammonia is a neutral donor, so the four ligands contribute nothing to the charge and the 2+ on the complex is the oxidation state of the copper. The sulfate outside the brackets is there only to balance that charge, and it is not attached to the metal, which is why it does not count towards the coordination number of 4. Reading the square brackets correctly settles both the charge question and the coordination number in one step.
questions.hint: Only what is inside the brackets is coordinated; count the ligands there and ignore the rest.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Coordination number of a metal carbonyl
questions.learningObjective: read the coordination number of a tetrahedral carbonyl
questions.stem: Nickel tetracarbonyl has the formula [Ni(CO)4] and a tetrahedral shape. What is its coordination number and what does the geometry tell you?

options.text: coordination number 2, because each carbon monoxide is treated as a pair
options.misconception: counts a coordinate bond as two sites rather than one

options.text: coordination number 8, because a carbonyl counts for two donor electrons
options.misconception: confuses donor electrons with donor atoms in the geometry count

options.text: coordination number 4, consistent with four positions in a tetrahedron
coordination number 6, because a tetrahedron encloses six ligand positions
options.misconception: counts the edges or faces of the polyhedron instead of its vertices

questions.explanation: The coordination number counts the ligands, and there are 4 carbonyls, each monodentate through its carbon, so the coordination number is 4. That number fixes the geometry: a four-coordinate complex is either tetrahedral or square planar, and here the ligand is small and the metal is in the zero oxidation state, so the tetrahedral arrangement is taken and the bond angles are 109.5 degrees. Counting donor electrons instead would give a different and useless number, since every metal-carbonyl bond happens to be a two-electron donation, and the coordination number would then be 8 for a tetrahedron that has only 4 vertices.
questions.hint: Count the ligands, then pick the geometry that has that many positions: 4 is tetrahedral or square planar.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Labile against inert complexes
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a kinetically labile complex from an inert one
questions.stem: A solution of a copper(II) aqua complex exchanges its water ligands within seconds, while a cobalt(III) ammine complex holds its ligands for hours. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: the copper complex is neutral and the cobalt complex is charged
options.misconception: believes overall charge sets substitution rate rather than the metal ion

options.text: the cobalt complex has more ligands, so each one binds more tightly
options.misconception: believes ligand count tightens bonds, when it is the metal that differs

options.text: the copper complex is in water and the cobalt complex is not
options.misconception: attributes a kinetic difference to the solvent the complex sits in

options.text: the cobalt(III) ion is a low-spin d6 ion with a large activation barrier

questions.explanation: Substitution rate is set by the activation barrier for breaking a metal-ligand bond, and that barrier depends on the electronic structure of the metal ion. Cobalt(III) is a d6 ion that, in an octahedral field, adopts a low-spin configuration with a completely filled set of t2g orbitals, so removing a ligand requires no promotion and costs a lot of energy, which is why its complexes are inert. Copper(II) is d9, its octahedral configuration carries an electron in an orbital that points at the ligands, and substitution is fast, which is why aqua copper solutions equilibrate almost at once. Nothing about charge, ligand count or solvent explains the difference.
questions.hint: Ask what the activation barrier for losing a ligand looks like for each d-electron configuration.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why a chelate is more stable than two monodentate ligands
questions.learningObjective: explain the chelate effect thermodynamically
questions.stem: A complex with two bidentate ligands is thermodynamically more stable than the analogous one with four monodentate ligands. What is the reason?

options.text: the bidentate ligands form stronger bonds per donor atom than monodentate ones
options.misconception: assumes donor atom bond strength rises with denticity, which is not the case

options.text: binding releases more particles, so the entropy of the solution rises
the bidentate ligands add more coordination sites and so raise the number
options.misconception: credits stability to a site count that is identical in the two complexes

options.text: the chelated complex has a lower charge and so attracts its counter-ions
options.misconception: invokes counter-ion attraction, which does not appear in the equilibrium

questions.explanation: Compare the two reactions: M + 2 NH3 -> M(NH3)2 consumes three particles to make one, while M + en -> M(en) consumes two to make one, so the chelated reaction has a larger increase in the number of free particles and a more positive entropy change. A larger entropy gain shifts the equilibrium to the complex, and since the enthalpy of the two is close to the same, the formation constant comes out larger. This is the chelate effect, and it is why ethylenediamine and the aminopolycarboxylates out-pull simple ammonia at the same donor atom count. The coordination numbers are identical in the two cases, so site count cannot be the explanation.
questions.hint: Write both formation equilibria with particles counted on each side, and look at the entropy.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Sigma and pi bonding in a metal carbonyl
questions.learningObjective: describe how a carbonyl binds a low-valent metal
questions.stem: Carbon monoxide binds a low-valent metal through both its sigma lone pair and a filled pi orbital. What does the second interaction do?

options.text: it adds a second coordination site, raising the coordination number
options.misconception: confuses a pi donation with a second donor atom, which would change the geometry

options.text: it transfers a proton to the metal, which is how metal hydrides form
options.misconception: describes a proton transfer, which is not part of carbonyl bonding

options.text: it puts electron density into the metal, which then back-donates in return
it breaks the carbon-oxygen bond and releases carbon monoxide atoms
options.misconception: believes the ligand dissociates, so nothing can be transferred

questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide donates its carbon lone pair into an empty metal orbital, which is an ordinary sigma donation and uses one coordination site. At the same time a filled pi orbital on the ligand donates into a metal orbital of matching symmetry, and the metal responds by back-donating from its own filled d orbitals into the ligand's empty pi star orbitals. The two directions reinforce each other, and the back-donation is what weakens the carbon-oxygen bond, which is why the carbon-oxygen stretching frequency falls on coordination. The geometry is set by the carbon atoms alone, so only the first interaction changes the coordination number.
questions.hint: Ask which way the electrons move in each direction, and what the metal gives back.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Two geometries for coordination number 8
questions.learningObjective: name the two common eight-coordinate geometries
questions.stem: Large metal ions with eight donor atoms around them are not rare. Which two arrangements account for almost all of them?

options.text: cubic and octahedral, the two arrangements of eight equal spheres
options.misconception: names a six-coordinate solid and a cube of eight vertices, one of which is rare

options.text: square antiprismatic and dodecahedral, the two eight-coordinate polyhedra
tetrahedral and square planar, the two arrangements of four sites doubled
options.misconception: names four-coordinate shapes and ignores the eight coordination number

options.text: hexagonal prism and pentagonal bipyramid, the two arrangements of eight
options.misconception: names a six-coordinate prism and a seven-coordinate shape instead

questions.explanation: With eight donor atoms the two arrangements that dominate are the square antiprism, a cube twisted so that every face is triangular, and the dodecahedron, whose faces are pentagons. Both give eight near-equivalent metal-ligand distances with a ligand-ligand repulsion close to the minimum, which is what matters when eight large donor atoms crowd the same centre. Square planar and tetrahedral describe four-coordinate centres, and a cubic arrangement of eight identical donors is a special case of the antiprism. The choice between the two eight-coordinate shapes is usually a small energy difference decided by the size and rigidity of the ligands.
questions.hint: Eight equal spheres pack best in two known ways; name both polyhedra.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Naming a cationic complex with mixed ligands
questions.learningObjective: assemble the IUPAC-style name of a cationic complex
questions.stem: A salt contains the complex [Co(NH3)5Cl]2+ with two chloride counter-ions. Which name follows the usual convention?

options.text: pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride, ligands first in alphabetical order
chloropentaamminecobalt(III) chloride, ligands in the order written in the formula
options.misconception: cites the ligands in formula order rather than alphabetically, so the name is not the convention

options.text: diamminetetraamminecobalt(III) chloride, counting the two counter-ions as ligands
options.misconception: counts the counter-ions as ligands and so doubles the coordination number

options.text: pentaamminechloridocobalt(II) chloride, taking the charge as the oxidation state
options.misconception: reads the 2+ charge of the complex as a metal oxidation state of 2

questions.explanation: The convention is: name the ligands first, alphabetically, with multiplicative prefixes, then the metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals, and finally the counter-ion as a separate word. Alphabetically ammine comes before chlorido, so the name is pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride, and the Roman numeral is 3 because the complex carries a 2+ charge with one chloride ligand of 1- inside the brackets. Formula order is not the rule, which is why chloropentaammine is wrong even though it describes the same thing, and the two outer chlorides are named once as chloride and are not ligands.
questions.hint: Ligands alphabetically with prefixes, then the metal and its Roman numeral, then the counter-ion.

questions.topic: Naming an anionic complex
questions.learningObjective: assemble the name of an anionic complex
questions.stem: The salt K4[Fe(CN)6] is to be named. Which statement about the name is correct?

options.text: tetrapotassium hexacyanidoiron(II), treating the cations as ligands
options.misconception: counts the potassium cations as ligands, which reverses the naming order

options.text: potassium hexacyanidoferric(II), using the cation to name the anion
options.misconception: keeps the neutral metal name in what is an anionic complex

options.text: potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II), with the metal name ending in -ate
potassium hexacyanidoferrate(IV), reading four potassium ions as the oxidation state
options.misconception: reads the number of counter-ions as the metal oxidation state

questions.explanation: An anionic complex takes the metal name with the ending -ate, so iron becomes ferrate, and the cationic counter-ion is named first as a separate word, so the salt is potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II). The Roman numeral is fixed by the charges: six cyanido ligands at 1- each need the metal at 2+ to give the 4- that four potassium ions require, which gives 2 + 6 = 8 of negative charge balanced by a 2+ metal. The four potassium ions are named once and are not ligands, and they say nothing directly about the oxidation state beyond fixing the total charge.
questions.hint: Anionic complex: -ate on the metal, cation first, Roman numeral from the charge balance.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Aqua against hydroxido ligands
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a water ligand from a hydroxide ligand
questions.stem: A chromium(III) complex in water slowly turns into a different complex. Which statement describes what has happened?

options.text: one H2O ligand has been replaced by a chloride from the solution
options.misconception: invents a chloride that is not present in the water

options.text: the chromium has been oxidised, so the charge on the complex is higher
options.misconception: claims an oxidation, whereas losing a proton raises no oxidation state

options.text: two aqua ligands have joined together to form a single bidentate ligand
options.misconception: describes ligand condensation, which does not occur in this step

options.text: one aqua ligand has lost a proton and become a hydroxido ligand

questions.explanation: Water is amphoteric, so a coordinated molecule can act as an acid and donate a proton, leaving a hydroxide ligand still attached to the metal. The chromium is untouched at +3 throughout, but the complex charge drops from 3+ to 2+ because one ligand is now anionic: six neutral waters give 3+ and five waters with one hydroxide give 2+. That drop of one unit in charge with no change of metal is the signature of a hydrolysis step, and it is why such solutions turn acidic on standing, since the released protons are not confined to the coordination sphere.
questions.hint: Compare the charges of the two formulas: the metal is the same, so a ligand must have changed.

questions.topic: Alphabetical order of ligands in a name
questions.learningObjective: order ligands alphabetically when assembling a name
questions.stem: A complex ion is written [Pt(NH3)3Cl3]+. Which is the correct order for the ligand part of its name?

options.text: triamminetrichlorido, because ammine sorts before chlorido
trichloridotriammine, because the ligands are named in formula order
options.misconception: keeps formula order, which is not the alphabetical rule the convention uses

options.text: triamminechlorido, because the repeated ligand is named only once
options.misconception: names a repeated ligand without its prefix, which loses the count

options.text: hexaamminechlorido, because all six positions are treated as one ligand
options.misconception: merges two different ligands into one name and loses the chlorides entirely

questions.explanation: Ligands are cited alphabetically, ignoring the multiplicative prefixes, so ammine sorts before chlorido and the name begins triamminetrichlorido. The prefixes themselves do the counting, and that is why they are ignored for the sort: if they were counted, tri would beat chlorido on some orderings and the rule would depend on the counts rather than the names. The platinum is +2, since three chlorides at 1- give a complex of 1+ only if the metal is 2+, so the full name is triamminetrichloridoplatinum(II), and the platinum sits in a square planar arrangement because the group number and oxidation state of a d8 ion make that the natural choice.
questions.hint: Sort the ligand names alphabetically, ignoring the tri-, di- and penta- type prefixes.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Multiplicative prefixes for ligand counts
questions.learningObjective: apply the multiplicative prefixes to ligand counts
questions.stem: How does the convention show that a complex contains three identical bidentate ligands?

options.text: by writing tri- before the bidentate ligand name
options.misconception: uses the tri- prefix, which the convention reserves for simpler ligand names

options.text: by writing tris- before the bidentate ligand name, since tri- is taken
options.misconception: invents a tris- prefix where the bracketed bis- form is used instead

options.text: by writing the bidentate name in brackets with a bis- prefix
by writing the bidentate ligand name three times in full
options.misconception: repeats the ligand name, which the multiplicative prefixes exist to avoid

questions.explanation: The multiplicative prefixes di-, tri- and tetra- are used for simple ligand names, but a ligand name that already contains a numerical prefix, or that is itself a two-part word, is placed in brackets and counted with bis-, tris- and tetrakis-. A bidentate ligand named ethane-1,2-diamine is multi-word, so three of them are written as tris(ethane-1,2-diamine), and a shorter polydentate name such as ethylenediamine takes bis(ethylenediamine). The bracket matters, because without it the reader cannot tell which word the count applies to.
questions.hint: A multi-word ligand name goes in brackets and is counted with bis- or tris-.

questions.topic: Cationic against anionic complex names
questions.learningObjective: choose the metal name ending from the charge of the complex
questions.stem: Two complexes are written [Co(NH3)6]3+ and [Co(CN)6]3-. How does the convention treat their metal names differently?

options.text: the cation takes -ate and the anion keeps the plain name
options.misconception: reverses the rule, giving -ate to the positively charged complex

options.text: both take -ate, because the ligands are all neutral in the second one
options.misconception: bases the ending on the ligands rather than on the charge of the complex

options.text: both keep the plain name, because -ate is used only for the metal itself
options.misconception: believes -ate applies to the element symbol rather than to the complex

options.text: the cation keeps cobalt and the anion becomes cobaltate

questions.topic: Roman numeral in a complex name
questions.learningObjective: explain what the Roman numeral in a complex name reports
questions.stem: In the name pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride, what does the Roman numeral report?

options.text: the coordination number, which is 6 for the complex named
options.misconception: confuses the coordination number with the oxidation state

options.text: the oxidation state of the metal, obtained by balancing all charges
the charge of the whole salt, which is neutral and so has no numeral
options.misconception: believes the Roman numeral reports the net charge of the salt

options.text: the number of counter-ions, which is 2 for this salt
options.misconception: believes the Roman numeral counts the outer anions

questions.topic: Formula that belongs to a stated name
questions.learningObjective: select the formula that matches a given complex name
questions.stem: A compound is named tetraamminecopper(II) sulfate with no water of crystallisation mentioned. Which formula is consistent with that name?

[Cu(NH3)4SO4], since sulfate is written inside the brackets
options.misconception: puts the counter-ion inside the coordination sphere, which the name forbids

questions.topic: Coordination isomerism
questions.learningObjective: identify coordination isomerism in a pair of salts
questions.stem: Two salts have the overall composition of one cobalt, five ammines, one bromide and one sulfate. What distinguishes them?

options.text: the first has the bromide inside the brackets and the second has it outside
options.misconception: describes the swap only one way, so it identifies a different pair of isomers

options.text: the two differ only in how many water molecules surround the cobalt
options.misconception: confuses coordination isomerism with hydrate isomerism

options.text: the bromide and the sulfate swap between the sphere and the counter-ion
the two differ in the oxidation state of the cobalt between them
options.misconception: believes the metal oxidation state changes when ligands move

questions.topic: Hydrate isomerism
questions.learningObjective: identify hydrate isomerism in hydrated salts
questions.stem: The salt CrCl3.6H2O exists in three distinct solid forms that differ in how many chlorides are coordinated. What is this called and why does it happen?

options.text: polymorphism, because the same solid takes up different crystal structures
options.misconception: confuses a change of crystal structure with a change of coordination sphere

options.text: hydrate isomerism, because water and chloride trade places inside the sphere
ionisation isomerism, because the counter-ion becomes a ligand and back
options.misconception: describes a different isomerism, which needs a coordinated anion to move out

questions.topic: Why octahedral splitting exceeds tetrahedral splitting

questions.stem: Explain why the d-orbital splitting in an octahedral complex is larger than in a tetrahedral one, and state one consequence.

answer.exemplar: Two things differ. In an octahedron six ligands lie along the axes, so two of the d orbitals, dz2 and dx2-y2, point directly at four ligands each and are pushed up hard, while the three t2g orbitals point between the ligands and fall. In a tetrahedron only four ligands are present, they are set at 109.5 degrees to one another, and none of them points along a d orbital, so the splitting has to come from the much smaller pi-type overlap that does occur. The net result is that delta-t is about four ninths of delta-o. The same counting gives the reversed order, since in a tetrahedron the two lower orbitals are the e set and the three upper are t2, and the shifts 2 x (-0.6) plus 3 x (0.4) cancel about the barycentre just as 3 x (-0.4) plus 2 x (0.6) do in the octahedron. The first consequence is that the small splitting makes tetrahedral complexes almost always high spin, since the energy gap to a raised orbital is smaller than the pairing energy, so the electrons occupy the upper set rather than pair up. The second is that tetrahedral complexes of a given d count are less strongly coloured, since a smaller gap absorbs light of longer wavelength, which lies further into the red and near the infrared.

questions.topic: Chelate effect as an entropy gain
questions.learningObjective: explain the chelate effect with a particle count
questions.stem: Explain why a complex with two bidentate ligands is more stable than the analogous complex with four monodentate ligands, counting the particles on each side of the two formation equilibria.

answer.exemplar: Write the two equilibria with every species shown. For monodentate ligands it is M + 4 NH3 -> M(NH3)4, which consumes five particles and produces one, a fall of four in the number of free species. For the chelate it is M + 2 en -> M(en)2, which consumes three particles and produces one, a fall of only two. Since the complexes themselves are almost the same size and the metal-ligand bonds are similar, the enthalpies of the two reactions are close, so the difference in equilibrium constant has to come mostly from entropy. Halving the fall in particle number at constant temperature and pressure means a noticeably larger entropy increase for the chelate formation, and because the Gibbs free energy is enthalpy minus T times entropy, a larger entropy term pushes the equilibrium further towards the complex. That is the chelate effect, and it is why ethylenediamine and the aminopolycarboxylates pull a metal out of solution at ligand concentrations at which ammonia leaves it behind. The two complexes have identical coordination numbers of 6, so the effect is not about how many sites are occupied but about how many separate molecules had to be taken out of solution to fill them.

Halving the fall in particle number at constant temperature and pressure means a noticeably larger entropy increase for the chelate formation, and because the Gibbs free energy is enthalpy minus T times entropy, a larger entropy term pushes the equilibrium further towards the complex. That is the chelate effect, and it is why ethylenediamine and the aminopolycarboxylates pull a metal out of solution at ligand concentrations at which ammonia leaves it behind. The two complexes have identical coordination numbers of 6, so the effect is not about how many sites are occupied but about how many separate molecules had to be taken out of solution to fill them.
